title: Solid full-cube block (cube_all / cube template)
rationale: A Java block whose model resolves to a single 0..16 cube maps directly to a Bedrock block with minecraft:material_instances and no geometry, because Bedrock renders a full cube by default.
limitations: Blockstate properties (axis, facing, powered, …) are not reproduced unless they are converted to Bedrock block states and permutations.

title: Cross-shaped plant block (cross / tinted_cross)
rationale: Java's cross template is two diagonal quads. Bedrock has no cross template, so the converter emits geometry 1.16.0 with two 45° planes, alpha_test rendering and no collision box.
limitations: Tinted cross models lose biome tinting; Bedrock applies tint only to vanilla plant blocks.
Plane thickness is a rendering aid, not part of the original model.

title: Orientable block with a distinct front face
rationale: Bedrock supports the minecraft:placement_direction trait with minecraft:cardinal_direction plus permutations, which reproduces the Java facing property and per-face front texture.
limitations: Only cardinal horizontal facings are reproduced; axis-based (up/down) orientable models need a separate state.

refs.title: Bedrock Wiki — Block Traits and permutations

title: Block with custom cuboid model elements
rationale: Java elements convert to Bedrock cubes (origin = java coordinate − 8 on X/Z, per-face uv → uv + uv_size). Rotation rescaling and multi-axis rotations cannot be expressed and are documented.
limitations: Element rotation with rescale is not representable in Bedrock geometry.
Models inheriting missing vanilla parents are approximated from whatever elements remain.

title: Block with additional blockstate properties
rationale: Bedrock blocks support custom states and permutations, but Java property semantics (e.g. redstone power levels, waterlogged, node types) need explicit per-property design that the converter cannot infer from blockstates alone.
limitations: Properties are listed in the report; the block converts with its default appearance only.
Redstone-powered variants require minecraft:redstone_conductivity plus per-state permutations.

title: Multipart blockstate (conditional model parts)
rationale: Java multipart combines conditional model parts (e.g. fences, redstone wire). Bedrock has no multipart model concept; parts must be modelled as separate geometry and toggled by permutations or replaced by vanilla-like behaviour.
limitations: Only the first multipart model is used for the Bedrock block appearance.

title: Block entity / machine block
rationale: Java BlockEntity classes hold per-block inventory, energy, fluid and tick logic. Bedrock block entities are not scriptable in stable builds for custom data, so machines must be rebuilt as entities with Script API, or approximated with vanilla containers.
limitations: Inventory, energy/fluid storage, processing progress and GUI are not reproduced automatically.
Ticking logic must be rewritten with the Script API (world.afterEvents / system.runInterval).

title: Translucent or cutout block (glass, ice, crystal)
rationale: Bedrock render_method controls blending: alpha_test for cutout, blend for translucent. Choosing blend for glass-like blocks preserves visible transparency.
limitations: Per-pixel alpha of the Java texture is honoured, but Bedrock's sorting of translucent blocks differs from Java.

title: Light-emitting block
rationale: Bedrock exposes minecraft:light_emission (0–15) per block, so the visual light level is reproducible once the Java value is known.
limitations: Java light values live in code; the converter infers 15 from the identifier and flags it as an assumption.
Light dampening and custom light colours are separate Bedrock components.

title: Block hardness and blast resistance
rationale: minecraft:destructible_by_mining.seconds_to_destroy and minecraft:destructible_by_explosion.explosion_resistance are the Bedrock equivalents of Java destroyTime/explosionResistance.
limitations: Values are taken from the conversion options (default 1.5 s) because Java hardness is set in code, not resources.

title: Slab / stairs / fence / wall shaped blocks
rationale: Shapes depend on Java model templates and, for fences/walls/stairs, neighbour connection logic that Bedrock implements only for its own block families. A generic conversion would look and behave wrong.
limitations: Reproduce as a custom block with matching geometry, or substitute the closest vanilla block family and document the difference.

title: Basic item with texture and max stack size
rationale: Bedrock items are data-driven: minecraft:icon references an item_texture.json shorthand, minecraft:max_stack_size and minecraft:display_name cover the common cases.
limitations: Item behaviour implemented in Java (right-click use, inventory logic) is not reproduced.

title: Tool item (sword, pickaxe, axe, shovel, hoe)
rationale: Bedrock items support minecraft:durability, minecraft:damage, minecraft:hand_equipped and minecraft:digger, which covers most tool behaviour without scripts.
limitations: Mining speed tiers and enchantability must be set explicitly; the converter uses iron-tier defaults and flags them.
Right-click special behaviour is code and is not converted.

refs.title: Bedrock Wiki — Item Components (durability, damage, digger)

title: Armor item (helmet, chestplate, leggings, boots)
rationale: minecraft:wearable with a slot and protection value, plus minecraft:durability, reproduces functional armor.
limitations: Custom armor models/attachable textures require an attachable definition and manual UV work.
Armor toughness and knockback resistance are not exposed as item components.

title: Food item
rationale: minecraft:food with nutrition, saturation_modifier and can_always_eat, plus minecraft:use_animation 'eat', reproduces the eating behaviour.
limitations: Java food effects (potion effects on eat) require minecraft:use_modifiers or Script API itemUse events.

title: Spawn egg item
rationale: Bedrock generates spawn eggs from the entity definition's is_spawnable flag and spawn_egg client-entity colours; no separate item JSON is needed.
limitations: Only works once the entity itself exists in the behaviour pack.

title: Bucket-style item (fluid container)
rationale: Bedrock buckets are implemented as items with a use action that places a fluid; the mapping between a custom fluid and a Bedrock block must be designed per mod.
limitations: Custom fluids have no Bedrock data equivalent; use existing water/lava or a Script API-driven block swap.

title: Item with durability / damage value
rationale: minecraft:durability max_durability maps to Java's max damage; minecraft:damage maps to attack damage.
limitations: Repair ingredients and enchantability need explicit components (minecraft:repairable, minecraft:enchantable).

title: Music disc / record item
rationale: Bedrock records need a sound event plus a jukebox_sound component; the audio file is usually shipped as an .ogg in the mod assets.
limitations: Audio must be registered in sounds.json and the item needs minecraft:record with a sound event id.

title: Item hidden from the creative inventory
rationale: Omitting menu_category in the Bedrock item description hides the item from creative, mirroring Java's absence from the creative tab.
limitations: The item must still be obtainable (recipe, loot, script) to be useful.

title: Shaped crafting recipe
rationale: Java pattern/key maps to Bedrock pattern/key directly; only the result and ingredient item ids need mapping.
limitations: Ingredient tags have no Bedrock equivalent and collapse to a representative item.
Recipe book grouping and unlock conditions do not exist on Bedrock.

title: Shapeless crafting recipe
rationale: minecraft:recipe_shapeless takes an ingredients array of item descriptors and a single result.
limitations: Alternative ingredients (lists) are collapsed to the first entry; Bedrock has no multi-item ingredient support in crafting recipes.

title: Smelting / blasting / smoking / campfire recipe
rationale: minecraft:recipe_furnace binds one input to one output and registered under the tags matching the block family (furnace, blast_furnace, smoker, campfire).
limitations: Cooking time and experience are not part of the Bedrock recipe; they belong to the block's behaviour.

title: Stonecutting recipe
rationale: Bedrock's minecraft:recipe_stonecutter takes one input descriptor and one result descriptor.
limitations: The count is part of the result descriptor on Bedrock, so multi-output stonecutting recipes need explicit counts.

title: Smithing transform recipe
rationale: minecraft:recipe_smithing_transform (template/base/addition/result) is the direct Bedrock equivalent of Java's smithing_transform.
limitations: Java recipes that omit the template need a template id chosen deliberately; the converter defaults to the netherite upgrade template and documents it.
smithing_trim has no Bedrock data equivalent.

title: Recipe ingredient using an item tag
rationale: Bedrock crafting recipes do not accept tags, so the converter substitutes a documented representative item (e.g. #minecraft:planks → minecraft:oak_planks).
limitations: Players lose the flexibility of crafting with any tag member.
Alternative for full fidelity: emit one recipe per tag member with distinct identifiers.

title: Custom RecipeSerializer recipe type
rationale: Java allows arbitrary recipe logic through RecipeSerializer implementations; Bedrock recipes are a fixed set of declarative types.
limitations: Reimplement the mechanic with a Script API block interaction, or approximate it with a standard recipe.

title: Custom mob entity
rationale: A structurally valid Bedrock entity can be generated with neutral wander/look behaviour, and the original texture reused when its UV layout happens to match the placeholder model.
limitations: AI goals, attributes, breeding/taming and animations are compiled Java code and are not reproduced.
The visual model is a labelled placeholder until rebuilt in Blockbench.

title: Projectile entity (arrow, fireball, thrown item)
rationale: Bedrock projectiles are entities with minecraft:projectile plus a shooter/splash component; Java projectile subclasses map conceptually but each parameter needs translation.
limitations: Damage, gravity, particle trail and impact effects must be set explicitly.

title: GeckoLib animated entity or block
rationale: GeckoLib uses its own JSON format for models and keyframe animations; Bedrock geometry/animation controllers are a different schema.
limitations: Rebuild the model in Blockbench and author animation controllers by hand.

title: Boss entity
rationale: Bedrock has a boss bar via the Script API (or the wither/dragon components), but phase logic and custom attacks are code.
limitations: Phases, attack patterns and boss bar behaviour need scripting.

title: Ore vein world generation
rationale: minecraft:ore_feature with count and replace_rules reproduces vein size and replacement targets; a feature_rules document places it.
limitations: Java placed_feature modifiers (height range, rarity, biome filters) are not translated automatically; the converter writes a uniform overworld distribution to be tuned.

refs.title: Bedrock Wiki — Intro to World Generation

title: Custom tree / vegetation feature
rationale: Bedrock tree features need a placed structure or a custom feature with explicit block placement; the parameter mapping from Java tree decorators is not implemented.
limitations: Recreate with a Bedrock tree feature, a structure, or a scripted generator.

title: Structure / jigsaw world generation
rationale: Bedrock structures are .mcstructure files placed by structure features; Java structure templates (NBT) can be converted block-by-block but not field-for-field.
limitations: NBT structure templates must be rebuilt or scripted into .mcstructure files.

title: Custom biome
rationale: Bedrock custom biomes require a biome JSON plus client-side biome definition and a world that opts into custom biomes; Java biome JSON differs in every field name.
limitations: Custom biomes are experimental-ish and only load under specific world settings.

title: Custom GUI screen
rationale: Java Screens render with immediate-mode GUI code; Bedrock has no client GUI API. The closest options are server forms (Script API @minecraft/server-ui) or a container entity.
limitations: Pixel-accurate layouts are not reproducible; behaviour must be redesigned as a form or container UI.

title: Container menu / inventory GUI
rationale: Java AbstractContainerMenu defines slots and syncing; Bedrock containers are fixed (chest, hopper, …) and custom slot layouts are not data-driven.
limitations: Use a chest/barrel entity or a scripted inventory model; slot layout cannot be matched exactly.

title: Mod configuration screen
rationale: Client config screens (Cloth Config, ModMenu) are Java-only UI.
limitations: Expose settings through a script form, world settings or a scoreboard-driven config.

title: Mixin / bytecode patch
rationale: Mixins rewrite vanilla Java classes at load time. Bedrock has no equivalent and none is planned; the behaviour must be reimplemented from scratch, often with the Script API.
limitations: Every mixin must be analysed by hand to determine what vanilla behaviour it changes.

title: Custom network packets
rationale: Java mods exchange custom payloads between client and server; Bedrock add-ons are server-authoritative data packs with no client channel.
limitations: Client-side effects must be approximated with particles, sounds and animations driven by scripts.

title: Custom command registration
rationale: The Bedrock Script API can register custom slash commands (system.beforeEvents.startup → customCommandRegistry), covering simple command behaviour.
limitations: Brigadier argument types, suggestions and client-side feedback need to be rebuilt.
Requires the beta script module in current versions.

title: Loader event subscriptions
rationale: Many Java events (block break, entity death, player tick) have Script API afterEvents counterparts.
limitations: Event ordering, cancellation and world tick timing differ; behaviour must be re-validated in game.

title: Item/block data components (1.20.5+)
rationale: Java data components attach typed data to items; Bedrock has a fixed component set plus item tags and dynamic properties via scripts.
limitations: Custom component semantics need a script-based representation (dynamic properties or lore/NBT-free tracking).

title: Custom redstone component
rationale: Bedrock blocks expose minecraft:redstone_conductivity, minecraft:redstone_consumer, minecraft:redstone_producer and per-state permutations.
limitations: Signal propagation quirks and update ordering differ from Java; validate with a redstone test rig.

title: Energy / fluid capability system
rationale: Java Forge/NeoForge capabilities and Fabric lookups are runtime interfaces with no data representation; Bedrock equivalents are scripted block entities or entity-based machines.
limitations: Design a script data model (dynamic properties per block position) for energy and fluid storage.

title: Custom particle effect
rationale: Bedrock particle JSON is a different schema from Java particle definitions but supports the same concepts (sprite, lifetime, motion, colour).
limitations: Rebuild each effect as a Bedrock particle_effect document; textures can often be reused.

title: Custom sound events
rationale: Bedrock sound_definitions.json registers .ogg files under a logical id; Java sound events map conceptually.
limitations: Sound categories and attenuation need explicit values; .ogg files can be copied if present in assets.

title: Custom loot table
rationale: Bedrock loot tables use pools/entries/functions similar to Java but with different function names.
limitations: Loot functions (set_count, enchant_randomly, …) need per-function translation; conditions differ.

title: Keybind / client input handling
rationale: Bedrock add-ons cannot register client keybinds; input must be expressed through items, blocks or forms.
limitations: Pick a gameplay action (item use, interaction) to replace the keybind.

title: Fabric mod structure
rationale: Fabric jars ship fabric.mod.json with id/version/depends, assets/<ns>/ and data/<ns>/ — enough to extract blocks, items, recipes and worldgen without running Java.
limitations: Registration code (Registry.register) is bytecode; the converter infers features from resources and lang keys.

title: Forge / NeoForge mod structure
rationale: Forge-family jars declare META-INF/mods.toml (or neoforge.mods.toml) with modId, version and [[dependencies]] blocks, and store assets/data in the same layout as Fabric.
limitations: Older 1.12-era mods use mcmod.info and numeric ids; support is best-effort.

title: External mod dependency
rationale: A mod that depends on another mod (GeckoLib, Create, Curios, …) inherits behaviour that the Bedrock add-on cannot reference.
limitations: Convert dependency mods first, or emulate the specific API surface the mod relies on.

title: Bedrock pack manifest requirements
rationale: Both BP and RP need format_version 2 manifests with unique header/module UUIDs, semver versions and min_engine_version; the BP can declare the RP as a dependency.
limitations: Reusing a UUID across two packs makes Minecraft ignore one of them; the converter derives deterministic UUIDs per mod and pack type.

title: Texture atlas registration
rationale: Block textures must appear in terrain_texture.json and item textures in item_texture.json; each entry maps a shorthand to a path under textures/.
limitations: Duplicate shorthands silently override each other, so keys are derived from the full namespaced id.

title: Translation keys for blocks and items
rationale: Bedrock resolves block names from tile.<identifier>.name and item names from item.<identifier>, read from texts/en_US.lang with a languages.json list.
limitations: Java keys use block.<ns>.<path>; the namespace separator changes from '.' to ':'.

title: Choosing format_version and min_engine_version
rationale: Component-based blocks/items require modern format versions (1.20.10+ for max_stack_size, 1.21.0 for current block components) and a matching min_engine_version in the manifest.
limitations: Too-new format versions fail to load on older clients; too-old ones ignore modern components.

title: item/generated model (flat sprite)
rationale: Java's item/generated is a flat sprite drawn from layer0; Bedrock item icons are flat sprites by default, so the texture maps 1:1.
limitations: Multi-layer generated models (e.g. tipped arrows, potions) need the layers composited or the Bedrock overlay/dyed icon support.

title: item/handheld model (held tool sprite)
rationale: minecraft:hand_equipped rotates the item in the player's hand, matching the Java handheld display transform closely.
limitations: Exact third-person transform angles are not configurable per item on Bedrock.

title: Manual validation checklist for converted packs
rationale: Automated checks can prove JSON validity and internal references, but blocks, items, recipes and entities must be exercised in a real Bedrock world.
limitations: Requires Minecraft Bedrock on Windows/Android/iOS with the pack imported as a world add-on.

title: Vanilla texture tile names differ between editions
rationale: A mod model may reference a vanilla texture that is not in the jar. Bedrock publishes those images under its own atlas tile names, and the naming is not a simple swap: Java says oak_planks/oak_log/oak_leaves while Bedrock says oak_planks/oak_log_side/oak_leaves. J2B verifies every tile it maps against the atlas files shipped in Mojang/bedrock-samples, so a mapping that Bedrock does not define is reported as a missing texture instead of being written into terrain_texture.json.
limitations: Only wood, wool and the identical-name families are mapped automatically; an unrecognised vanilla reference is reported, not guessed.

title: Borrowing a vanilla tile without redistributing it
rationale: When a block uses vanilla art, the resource pack declares the atlas key and points it at the path the vanilla pack already ships (textures/blocks/oak_planks). No PNG is copied, so Mojang's art is not redistributed, and the key resolves because Bedrock looks the entry up by path.
limitations: Validation accepts these entries without a local file only when the key exists in the official vanilla atlas; any other dangling path is still an error.

refs.title: Microsoft Learn — resource pack texture atlas

title: One PNG serving both the block and item atlases
rationale: A block texture reused as an item icon is copied once and registered in both terrain_texture.json and item_texture.json, because Bedrock resolves each atlas independently.
limitations: The icon keeps the block texture's own resolution; no icon-specific padding or recolouring is applied.

title: Item icon resolved through the model inheritance chain
rationale: A Java item model often declares no textures and reaches a block or custom model several parents up. J2B walks the same chain the block converter uses and takes the first texture that resolves, instead of falling back to a vanilla stick icon.
limitations: A 3D item model is still reduced to its icon; the equipped model needs an attachable and is reported separately.

title: Convention tags (c:/forge:) with no tag file in the jar
rationale: Fabric and NeoForge ship loader-wide convention tags under data/c/ and data/neoforge/. Their files are usually absent from a single mod's jar, so the tag is invisible unless the converter indexes those namespaces and has a representative for the tag. J2B scans every namespace that ships tags, then substitutes the documented single vanilla item for tags such as c:dusts/redstone or c:ingots/iron, recording the substitution as a loss.
limitations: A tag with several members is reduced to one member, so only that member crafts. Tags with no documented representative are still dropped, and the recipe is reported rather than rewritten.

title: Blockstate rotations baked into geometry instead of transformation
rationale: A quarter turn of an axis-aligned box is still an axis-aligned box, so a blockstate's x/y model rotation is applied to the cube coordinates and emitted as a separate geometry. This avoids minecraft:transformation, whose pivot and axis conventions are easy to get subtly wrong.
limitations: Every distinct rotation needs its own geometry file, which multiplies pack size for blocks with many orientations. Non-quarter-turn variant rotations cannot be baked and are reported.

title: Blockstate model rotation baked into geometry
rationale: Java states a model rotation per variant (x then y, in 90-degree steps). A quarter turn of an axis-aligned box is still an axis-aligned box, so the rotation is baked into the exported cubes and face names instead of using minecraft:transformation, whose axis order is easy to get wrong. x=90 tilts +y onto -z (north); y=90 turns +x (east) onto +z (south), which is why vanilla stairs use y=0 for facing=east and y=90 for facing=south.
limitations: Source: Minecraft Java blockstate definition (x, y, uvlock). Bedrock rotation baking keeps UVs glued to their face, so a non-square UV region is correct only if the face survives the turn unchanged.
Rotations that are not quarter turns cannot be expressed by baked cuboids and are reported instead of approximated.

title: Item icon borrowed from a vanilla item tile
rationale: An item model may point at minecraft:item/stick, which is not in the mod jar. Bedrock resolves item icons through item_texture.json, and resource packs merge their atlas with vanilla's, so the converted item can name the vanilla tile directly. The path is taken from the official atlas instead of being rebuilt as textures/items/<key>, because vanilla keeps some tiles in subfolders.
limitations: The icon is the vanilla tile, not a copy: another pack that overrides that tile changes this item too.
No attachment, use animation or durability bar comes from the icon alone.
